CourseName: CEN3722 - Introduction to Human Computer Interfaces

Outcomes.Text: Explain the purpose and structure of a professional HCI development report.
Identify the key sections required to document a full HCI design process.
Apply evidence-linking techniques to connect design decisions to measurable outcomes.
Analyze design decisions made at each stage from requirements gathering through final implementation.
Demonstrate how to document evaluation findings and reflect them in iterative design revisions.
Create a comprehensive group development report that traces the complete HCI design process.

Topics.Title: Introduction to HCI Development Reporting
Topics.Summary: Establishes the purpose of professional HCI development reports and explains how they function as a traceable record of design decision-making from start to finish.

Elements.Title: Purpose of an HCI Development Report
Elements.BodyText: An HCI development report provides a structured, professional account of the entire design process, communicating decisions, rationale, and outcomes to stakeholders.
Elements.Notes: Emphasize that the report is not simply a record of what was done but a justified narrative explaining why each decision was made and what evidence supports it.

Items.Text: The report serves as a traceable document linking design decisions to user requirements and evaluation outcomes.
It demonstrates professional practice by showing systematic, evidence-based design thinking.
Stakeholders use the report to assess the rigor and quality of the HCI process.

Elements.Title: Audience and Tone
Elements.BodyText: A professional HCI report is written for a technically informed audience and must maintain a formal, objective tone throughout.
Elements.Notes: Students often default to informal language when describing collaborative group work; remind them that even process descriptions should use professional academic register.

Items.Text: Reports should be written for readers who understand HCI principles but may not be familiar with the specific project.
Formal, objective language is required even when describing iterative or exploratory design activities.
Avoid first-person narrative in favor of passive constructions or third-person references to the team.

Elements.Title: Report as a Design Artefact
Elements.BodyText: The development report itself is considered a design artefact, representing the intellectual and practical work of the project team.
Elements.Notes: This framing helps students understand that the quality of documentation reflects the quality of their design practice, not just a post-hoc write-up.

Items.Text: A well-structured report demonstrates that the team followed a principled HCI methodology.
The report provides an auditable trail of decisions that others could replicate or critique.
Completeness and coherence of the report are as important as the interface prototype itself.

Topics.Title: Requirements Documentation
Topics.Summary: Covers how to document the requirements-gathering phase, including user needs, functional and non-functional requirements, and the rationale for design constraints.

Elements.Title: Documenting User Research
Elements.BodyText: The report must describe the methods used to gather user needs, including observations, interviews, surveys, or contextual inquiry, along with key findings.
Elements.Notes: Include participant demographics, recruitment criteria, and any ethical considerations such as informed consent in this section.

Items.Text: Specify the research method used and justify why it was appropriate for the target user group.
Summarize key user needs and pain points identified through the research activities.
Include anonymized data samples or quotes as evidence to support stated user needs.

Elements.Title: Stating Functional and Non-Functional Requirements
Elements.BodyText: Requirements must be clearly categorized as functional or non-functional and written in precise, testable language.
Elements.Notes: Functional requirements describe what the system must do; non-functional requirements describe quality attributes such as performance, accessibility, or usability standards.

Items.Text: Each functional requirement should specify a discrete system behavior or capability.
Non-functional requirements must reference measurable criteria wherever possible.
Requirements should be numbered to allow traceability to later design and evaluation sections.

Elements.Title: Rationale for Design Constraints
Elements.BodyText: Any constraints placed on the design — such as platform, accessibility standards, or scope limitations — must be explicitly stated and justified.
Elements.Notes: Constraints often arise from user research, client briefs, or technical limitations and should be treated as design inputs rather than restrictions.

Items.Text: Constraints should be distinguished from requirements and explained in terms of their source.
The impact of each constraint on subsequent design decisions should be acknowledged.
Referencing recognized standards such as WCAG provides credibility to accessibility constraints.

Elements.Title: Linking Requirements to Design Goals
Elements.BodyText: The report should show how gathered requirements were translated into concrete design goals that guided the project.
Elements.Notes: A simple traceability matrix or numbered cross-references between requirements and design decisions can serve this purpose effectively.

Items.Text: Design goals should be derived directly from identified user needs and stated requirements.
Each design goal should be specific enough to evaluate against in later testing phases.
Demonstrating this linkage shows that design decisions were user-centered rather than arbitrary.

Topics.Title: Design Process Documentation
Topics.Summary: Explains how to document the iterative design process, including concept generation, design rationale, low- and high-fidelity prototyping, and the evolution of design decisions.

Elements.Title: Documenting Concept Generation
Elements.BodyText: The report should describe early ideation activities, such as sketching, brainstorming, or design workshops, and explain how initial concepts were generated and evaluated.
Elements.Notes: Include photographs of sketches, affinity diagrams, or other ideation outputs as appendix evidence referenced from the main text.

Items.Text: Describe the ideation method used and the criteria applied to assess initial concepts.
Explain how team members contributed to concept generation and how divergent ideas were reconciled.
Show which concepts were selected for further development and why others were discarded.

Elements.Title: Describing Low-Fidelity Prototypes
Elements.BodyText: Low-fidelity prototypes such as paper sketches or wireframes must be documented with annotated images and an explanation of what each prototype was intended to test.
Elements.Notes: Low-fidelity prototypes are used to explore layout and navigation early and cheaply; the report should make clear that these were testing tools, not final designs.

Items.Text: Include annotated images of each low-fidelity prototype in the report or appendices.
Explain the specific design questions or hypotheses each prototype was created to explore.
Describe any informal feedback gathered during the low-fidelity phase and how it shaped subsequent iterations.

Elements.Title: Documenting Design Rationale
Elements.BodyText: Design rationale explains why specific design choices were made, grounding decisions in HCI principles, guidelines, or user research evidence.
Elements.Notes: Reference established HCI guidelines such as Nielsen's heuristics or Shneiderman's eight golden rules where applicable to strengthen the rationale.

Items.Text: Each significant design decision should be accompanied by a stated rationale.
Rationale should reference either user research findings, HCI principles, or both.
Avoid describing what was designed without also explaining why that choice was made.

Elements.Title: Describing High-Fidelity Prototypes
Elements.BodyText: High-fidelity prototypes represent near-final interface designs and should be documented with annotated screenshots and a clear account of how they differ from earlier iterations.
Elements.Notes: Highlight design improvements made in response to earlier feedback, showing the iterative nature of the process.

Items.Text: Document key interface screens with annotated screenshots cross-referenced in the text.
Explain what was changed between the low-fidelity and high-fidelity versions and why.
Describe the tools and technologies used to create the high-fidelity prototype.

Elements.Title: Capturing Design Evolution
Elements.BodyText: The report should present the design process as an iterative journey, showing how early decisions were refined in response to evaluation findings and emerging insights.
Elements.Notes: A timeline or version history table can help communicate iteration stages clearly and concisely.

Items.Text: Use a structured narrative or visual timeline to show how the design evolved across iterations.
Explicitly link each design change to the evidence or feedback that motivated it.
Avoid presenting the design as if it emerged fully formed; iteration is evidence of rigorous practice.

Topics.Title: Evaluation Documentation
Topics.Summary: Describes how to document usability evaluations and user testing activities, including methodology, findings, and the implications of results for design decisions.

Elements.Title: Documenting Evaluation Methodology
Elements.BodyText: The report must specify the evaluation method used, such as usability testing, heuristic evaluation, or cognitive walkthrough, along with the rationale for selecting that method.
Elements.Notes: Justify the choice of evaluation method in relation to the design stage, available resources, and the specific usability questions being investigated.

Items.Text: Name and define the evaluation method and explain why it was appropriate at this stage.
Describe the participants involved, including recruitment criteria and any ethical protocols followed.
Specify the tasks, scenarios, or heuristics used during the evaluation session.

Elements.Title: Presenting Evaluation Findings
Elements.BodyText: Findings from evaluation activities must be presented clearly, distinguishing between observed problems, participant feedback, and analyst interpretations.
Elements.Notes: Use tables, severity ratings, or thematic groupings to organize findings for readability; avoid burying key results in dense prose.

Items.Text: Separate factual observations from interpretive conclusions in the findings section.
Quantitative data such as task completion rates or error frequencies should be presented with appropriate metrics.
Qualitative feedback such as participant quotes should be anonymized and used as supporting evidence.

Elements.Title: Linking Evaluation Findings to Design Iterations
Elements.BodyText: The report must explicitly connect evaluation findings to subsequent design changes, demonstrating that evaluation informed and improved the design.
Elements.Notes: This linkage is critical for demonstrating a truly iterative, user-centered design process rather than a linear one.

Items.Text: For each significant usability problem identified, describe the design change made in response.
If a finding did not result in a design change, provide a reasoned justification for the decision.
Use cross-references between the evaluation and design sections to reinforce traceability.

Elements.Title: Reflecting on Evaluation Limitations
Elements.BodyText: A professional report acknowledges the limitations of its evaluation activities, such as small sample sizes, time constraints, or method choices that may affect the validity of findings.
Elements.Notes: Acknowledging limitations demonstrates academic maturity and critical reflection; it does not undermine the report but strengthens its credibility.

Items.Text: Identify specific limitations in participant recruitment, task design, or evaluation environment.
Explain how identified limitations may have influenced the findings or their generalizability.
Suggest how future evaluations could address these limitations with more resources or time.

Topics.Title: Final Implementation Documentation
Topics.Summary: Explains how to document the final implemented design, including a description of the interface, design decisions made during implementation, and any deviations from the prototype.

Elements.Title: Describing the Final Interface
Elements.BodyText: The final implementation section presents the delivered interface design, using annotated screenshots or walkthroughs to describe its key features and interactions.
Elements.Notes: Organize the description around user tasks or system features rather than simply listing screens in order.

Items.Text: Provide annotated screenshots of each key screen or interaction state in the final interface.
Describe how the interface supports the core user tasks identified in the requirements phase.
Reference relevant design principles or guidelines that informed the final design decisions.

Elements.Title: Documenting Implementation Decisions
Elements.BodyText: Any design decisions made specifically during the implementation phase must be documented, including choices about interaction patterns, visual design, or technical constraints.
Elements.Notes: Implementation often surfaces new constraints not visible at the prototype stage; documenting these decisions shows that the team responded thoughtfully to real-world challenges.

Items.Text: Explain any decisions made during implementation that were not anticipated at the prototype stage.
Justify implementation choices in terms of usability, technical feasibility, or design consistency.
Describe how implementation decisions were evaluated against the original design goals.

Elements.Title: Documenting Deviations from the Prototype
Elements.BodyText: Where the final implementation differs from the approved prototype, the report must explain the reasons for any deviations and assess their impact on usability.
Elements.Notes: Deviations are not failures; documenting them honestly and with justification demonstrates professional integrity and reflective practice.

Items.Text: List any features or design elements that changed during implementation relative to the prototype.
Provide a clear rationale for each deviation, whether technical, time-based, or usability-driven.
Assess whether each deviation affected the ability of the design to meet its original requirements.

Elements.Title: Tracing Design Decisions to Outcomes
Elements.BodyText: The implementation section should close by demonstrating how the final design addresses the requirements and design goals established at the start of the project.
Elements.Notes: A traceability matrix mapping requirements to implemented features and evaluation evidence is a highly effective tool for this purpose.

Items.Text: Show explicitly how each major requirement is addressed in the final implementation.
Reference evaluation evidence that confirms the design meets stated usability goals.
Acknowledge any requirements that were only partially met and explain the circumstances.

Topics.Title: Group Collaboration and Contribution Documentation
Topics.Summary: Covers how a group development report should document team collaboration, individual contributions, and the processes used to manage the design project collectively.

Elements.Title: Documenting Team Roles and Responsibilities
Elements.BodyText: The report should identify the roles taken by each team member and describe how responsibilities were allocated across the project phases.
Elements.Notes: Role descriptions should be specific and activity-based rather than vague; avoid generic labels like 'researcher' without describing what that role entailed.

Items.Text: Describe each team member's role with reference to specific tasks and project phases.
Explain the rationale behind the division of labor, including any changes made during the project.
Acknowledge overlapping responsibilities and collaborative activities where relevant.

Elements.Title: Describing Collaborative Design Processes
Elements.BodyText: The report should describe how the team made collective design decisions, including any structured processes such as design critiques, team reviews, or voting methods.
Elements.Notes: Documenting collaborative processes demonstrates that design decisions were deliberated rather than made unilaterally by one team member.

Items.Text: Describe the methods used to reach agreement on key design decisions within the team.
Reference any structured review or critique sessions that influenced the design direction.
Explain how disagreements or competing ideas were resolved during the design process.

Elements.Title: Documenting Project Management Activities
Elements.BodyText: Brief documentation of project management activities such as scheduling, task tracking, and version control demonstrates professional practice.
Elements.Notes: Include references to tools used, such as Trello, GitHub, or shared design platforms, as evidence of organized collaborative working.

Items.Text: Describe the tools and methods used to manage tasks, deadlines, and deliverables.
Explain how version control or file management was handled across the team.
Reflect on the effectiveness of the project management approach and any adjustments made.

Elements.Title: Reflecting on Group Process
Elements.BodyText: The report should include a reflective component in which the team honestly evaluates the effectiveness of their collaborative process.
Elements.Notes: Reflection should be balanced, acknowledging both what worked well and what could be improved, grounded in specific examples from the project.

Items.Text: Identify specific strengths in the team's collaborative process with supporting examples.
Acknowledge challenges encountered during collaboration and describe how they were managed.
Suggest concrete improvements the team would implement in a future similar project.

Topics.Title: Report Structure, Referencing, and Presentation
Topics.Summary: Provides guidance on the structural conventions, academic referencing requirements, and professional presentation standards expected in an HCI development report.

Elements.Title: Standard Report Structure
Elements.BodyText: An HCI development report follows a conventional academic and professional structure that includes front matter, a body organized by project phase, and supporting appendices.
Elements.Notes: Typical sections include: title page, abstract, table of contents, introduction, requirements, design process, evaluation, final implementation, reflection, references, and appendices.

Items.Text: Include front matter such as a title page, abstract, and table of contents as standard professional elements.
Organize the body of the report to mirror the chronological stages of the HCI design process.
Place supporting evidence such as raw data, consent forms, and additional prototypes in clearly labeled appendices.

Elements.Title: Writing Cohesive Narratives Across Sections
Elements.BodyText: Each section of the report must connect logically to adjacent sections, ensuring the overall document reads as a coherent account of an integrated design process.
Elements.Notes: Use transitional summaries at the end of each section to signal what the next section will address and how it relates to what came before.

Items.Text: Use explicit cross-references to link related content across different sections of the report.
Begin each major section with a brief statement of its purpose and its relationship to the preceding section.
Avoid treating each section as a standalone document; the report must flow as a unified narrative.

Elements.Title: Academic Referencing
Elements.BodyText: All sources cited in the report, including HCI guidelines, design principles, and research methods, must be referenced using the required academic referencing style.
Elements.Notes: Consistent and accurate referencing demonstrates academic integrity and enables readers to locate and verify the sources underpinning design decisions.

Items.Text: Cite HCI principles, guidelines, and theoretical frameworks used to justify design decisions.
Follow the prescribed referencing style consistently throughout the report.
Include a complete reference list at the end of the document formatted according to the required style.

Elements.Title: Use of Visual Evidence
Elements.BodyText: Figures, screenshots, diagrams, and tables must be used strategically to support written arguments and are subject to the same presentation standards as text.
Elements.Notes: Every figure must be numbered, captioned, and explicitly referenced in the body text; orphaned figures with no textual discussion undermine report quality.

Items.Text: Number and caption all figures, tables, and diagrams consistently throughout the report.
Reference every visual element explicitly in the body text at the point it becomes relevant.
Ensure all images are of sufficient resolution and clarity to communicate their intended content.

Elements.Title: Presentation and Formatting Standards
Elements.BodyText: Professional formatting — including consistent fonts, heading hierarchies, appropriate line spacing, and accurate word counts — reflects the quality of the team's work.
Elements.Notes: Inconsistent formatting across group-authored sections is a common issue; establish a shared style guide or template before writing begins.

Items.Text: Apply a consistent heading hierarchy and typography style throughout the entire document.
Adhere to any specified word count limits, distributing the count appropriately across sections.
Conduct a final formatting review to eliminate inconsistencies arising from multiple authors.
